Authorities: IMA CMA Exam Content Specification Outline - Decision Analysis

Choices.A: ACCEPT - net +$48,000 after the November overtime premium caused by the October squeeze
Choices.C: Reject - October is full, full stop
Choices.D: Reject - rush orders never justify overtime

CommonTrapReference: Trap DA-T09: Single-period framing that hides cross-month displacement costs
ExplanationCorrect: Incremental October contribution from the rush order = 2,000 units x ($70 - $40) = $60,000. Accepting fills October capacity that would otherwise run 2,000 regular units, pushing them into November overtime at a $6 per unit premium: displacement cost = 2,000 x $6 = $12,000. Net effect across the two months = $60,000 - $12,000 = +$48,000, so ACCEPT. The timing insight is that the true marginal cost of filling October arrives next month as premium labor, not in the month of sale. Trap: booking the full $60,000 while ignoring downstream consequences, or rejecting categorically because the current month appears full.
ExplanationWrongB: Option B books the full $60,000 and never traces the $12,000 November overtime premium that the October squeeze creates; the honest net gain is $48,000.
ExplanationWrongC: Option C rejects because October is committed; commitment is not the test, because the order still adds $48,000 net across the window after absorbing its own displacement cost.
ExplanationWrongD: Option D applies a blanket prohibition against overtime; differential analysis prices this specific trade at positive $48,000, so the categorical rule destroys measurable value.
Stem: October production committed (8,000 units); rush order 2,000 units at $70 (VC $40) wants October delivery; accepting pushes 2,000 November regular units into overtime at a $6 premium. Accept?
VerifiedChecks: Independent: 60K October gain - 12K Nov premium = +48K accept

Authorities: Drop/keep differential analysis with exit obligations
IMA CMA Exam Content Specification Outline - Decision Analysis

Choices.B: +$70,000 - net of the warranty tail AND the one-time write-off

CommonTrapReference: Trap DA-T10: Exit costs omitted or sign-flipped in drop decisions
ExplanationCorrect: Dropping the legacy product releases $150,000 of annual variable and dedicated fixed costs. Exit obligations offset part of that relief in year one: committed warranty service continues at $40,000 per year for five years, and closing the line triggers a one-time $60,000 inventory write-off. Year-one net saving = $150,000 - $40,000 - $60,000 = +$70,000. Interpretation: the discontinuation improves year-one results, but the warranty tail carries $40,000 forward annually, so years two through five save $110,000 each. Trap: crediting the full cost release while forgetting exit obligations, or netting the penalties with reversed signs.
ExplanationWrongA: Option A claims the entire $150,000 release and ignores both the $40,000 warranty tail and the $60,000 write-off; year-one relief shrinks to $70,000 once exit obligations are priced.
ExplanationWrongC: Option C deducts the warranty service but forgets the one-time $60,000 inventory write-off triggered by closure; including it lowers year-one net saving from $110,000 to $70,000.
ExplanationWrongD: Option D flips signs and sums the $40,000 tail with the $60,000 write-off against no offsetting benefit, printing -$50,000; the $150,000 release dominates and the true year-one effect is +$70,000.
Stem: Discontinuing saves variable and dedicated fixed costs of $150K per year; committed warranty service runs $40K per year for five years; closure triggers a one-time inventory write-off of $60K. YEAR-ONE net saving?
Topic: C.195 Warranty tail in a drop decision

Authorities: IMA CMA Exam Content Specification Outline - Decision Analysis

Choices.A: Strategy F - the safest floor dominates any weighted blend
Choices.B: Strategy E - balanced scores win by default
Choices.C: STRATEGY D - Hurwicz weight 0.7 x $90K plus 0.3 x (-$20K) = $57K, ahead of E ($49K) and F ($48K)

CommonTrapReference: Trap DA-T11: Criterion substitution - maximin or maximax answers a Hurwicz question
ExplanationCorrect: The Hurwicz criterion scores each strategy as alpha x best payoff + (1 - alpha) x worst payoff. With alpha = 0.7: Strategy D = 0.7($90K) + 0.3(-$20K) = $63K - $6K = $57K; Strategy E = 0.7($70K) + 0.3($0) = $49K; Strategy F = 0.7($60K) + 0.3($20K) = $42K + $6K = $48K. Select STRATEGY D at $57K. An alpha of 0.7 signals a decision maker leaning toward upside while still pricing downside at 30% weight. Trap: substituting maximin (which crowns F for its $20K floor) or maximax (which chases the largest best case) instead of computing the required weighted blend.
ExplanationWrongA: Option A lets the $20K worst-case floor of Strategy F dominate; that is maximin logic, not Hurwicz - F blends to just $48K under the 0.7 / 0.3 weights, last in the ranking.
ExplanationWrongB: Option B rewards balance without doing the arithmetic; E computes to 0.7($70K) + 0.3($0) = $49K, trailing D by $8K.
ExplanationWrongD: Option D declares a tie at $57K; only D reaches $57K, with E at $49K and F at $48K, so the ordering is strict and unique.
Stem: Alpha 0.7 optimism. Strategy D: best $90K worst -$20K; E: best $70K worst $0; F: best $60K worst $20K. Which strategy does Hurwicz select?

Authorities: Expected-value analysis for risk transfer decisions
IMA CMA Exam Content Specification Outline - Decision Analysis

Choices.B: $1,500 - summing rather than weighting the penalties
Choices.D: $1,000 EXPECTED PENALTY - pay the $750 guarantee and save $250 per shipment in expectation

CommonTrapReference: Trap DA-T12: Scenario outcomes summed without probability weights
ExplanationCorrect: Expected penalty per shipment = 0.10 x (1 late day x $5,000) + 0.05 x (2 late days x $5,000) = $500 + $500 = $1,000. The guaranteed-service upgrade costs a certain $750, so switching saves $1,000 - $750 = $250 per shipment in expectation. A risk-neutral shipper buys the guarantee whenever its certain cost sits below the expected penalty it extinguishes; here the margin is a clear $250. Interpretation: probabilistic exposure of $1,000 per shipment is replaced by a $750 certain cost. Trap: adding scenario penalties without their probabilities, or counting only the single-day event and understating exposure.
ExplanationWrongA: Option A weights only the 10% single-day event ($500) and discards the 5% two-day event, which contributes another $500; full expected exposure is $1,000.
ExplanationWrongB: Option B smears the combined 15% late-event probability across the $10,000 two-day penalty (0.15 x $10,000 = $1,500); correct weighting separates events: 0.10($5,000) + 0.05($10,000) = $1,000.
ExplanationWrongC: Option C calls $750 the break-even, confusing the guarantee price with the expected penalty; the expectation is $1,000, so the switch banks a $250 expected saving rather than parity.
Stem: Carrier promises 2-day delivery, $5,000 penalty per late day; history 10 percent chance 1 late day, 5 percent chance 2 late days; guaranteed upgrade costs $750. Expected penalty and decision?

Authorities: Cost-volume-profit breakeven applied to market share
IMA CMA Exam Content Specification Outline - Decision Analysis

Choices.A: 20.0% - breakeven volume of 400,000 units against a 2,000,000-unit market

CommonTrapReference: Trap DA-T13: Unit-versus-dollar confusion in market-share breakeven
ExplanationCorrect: Break-even units = fixed costs / unit contribution = $6,400,000 / $16 = 400,000 units. Required market share = 400,000 / 2,000,000 = 20.0%. Interpretation: the plan survives only if the firm captures one in five units sold in the region, a demanding entry threshold that should prompt scrutiny of price, cost structure, or market definition before launch. Trap: mixing dollar fixed costs with unit volumes without converting, or forming the share ratio before the unit requirement exists.
ExplanationWrongB: Option B prints 32.0%; recomputation gives $6,400,000 / $16 = 400,000 break-even units and 400,000 / 2,000,000 = 20.0%, so the printed share overstates the requirement by more than half.
ExplanationWrongC: Option C prints 12.8%; the correct chain divides fixed costs by the $16 contribution first (400,000 units) and only then forms the market ratio, landing at 20.0%.
ExplanationWrongD: Option D prints 3.2%; this drops a factor of scale between the $6.4 million pool and unit volumes, while $6,400,000 / $16 = 400,000 units equals 20.0% of the market.
Stem: Regional market 2,000,000 units; fixed costs $6.4M; contribution $16 per unit. Breakeven market share?

Authorities: IMA CMA Exam Content Specification Outline - Decision Analysis

Choices.A: $1,364,000 - fee computed on a base including the excluded $80K
Choices.B: $1,284,000 - seven percent of the compliant $1.2M base, added back
Choices.D: $84,000 - the fee alone is the price

CommonTrapReference: Trap DA-T14: Unallowable costs leaked into the fee base
ExplanationCorrect: Under a cost-plus-fixed-fee arrangement, the contractor recovers ALLOWED cost and earns a fee expressed as a percentage of that same allowed base. The bid included $80,000 of lobbying and entertainment that contract rules exclude, so the compliant allowed base is $1,200,000. Contract price = $1,200,000 x 1.07 = $1,284,000. Interpretation: unallowable costs stay with the contractor and cannot leak into the fee base; padding the base by $80,000 would raise the price by $85,600 ($80,000 of barred cost plus $5,600 of extra fee). Trap: computing the 7% fee on a base padded with excluded items, or reading cost-plus as fee-free reimbursement.
ExplanationWrongA: Option A folds the disallowed $80,000 back into the recovery; excluded lobbying and entertainment belong to the contractor, and the compliant $1,200,000 base prices the job at $1,284,000.
ExplanationWrongC: Option C reads cost-plus as pure reimbursement with no markup; the fixed fee of 7% rides on top of allowed cost, lifting the price to $1,284,000.
ExplanationWrongD: Option D offers the $84,000 fee ($1,200,000 x 0.07) as the whole price; the fee supplements recovered cost, so the contractor collects $1,284,000 in total.
Stem: Fee = 7 percent of ALLOWED cost; bid included $80K lobbying and entertainment excluded by rules; compliant base $1.2M. Contract PRICE?

Authorities: Theory of Constraints optimization with outsourcing option (integrative)
IMA CMA Exam Content Specification Outline - Decision Analysis

Choices.A: $25,500 - refusing the vendor because its premium erodes margin
Choices.B: $29,900 - but outsourcing P1 production instead of P2
Choices.C: $29,900 TOTAL - honor the 100-unit P1 floor (150 hours), run P2 in-house to demand (350 hours -> 700 units), and outsource the residual 200 P2 units at $22 net each

CommonTrapReference: Trap DA-T15: Ranking by unit contribution instead of contribution per constraint hour
ExplanationCorrect: Rank the constraint: in-house P2 earns $30 / 0.5 = $60 per constraint hour (top priority); in-house P1 earns $45 / 1.5 = $30 per hour; outsourced P2 bypasses the constraint and nets $30 - $8 = $22 per unit. The contractual floor forces 100 units of P1 first, consuming 150 hours. The remaining 350 hours go to in-house P2: 350 / 0.5 = 700 units, leaving 200 of its 900-unit demand unserved, which moves to the vendor at $22 net. Total contribution = (100 x $45) + (700 x $30) + (200 x $22) = $4,500 + $21,000 + $4,400 = $29,900. Trap: ranking products by unit contribution instead of contribution per constraint hour, or refusing outsourcing outright and stranding real demand.
ExplanationWrongA: Option A refuses the vendor on premium grounds and strands 200 units of P2 demand; contribution collapses to $25,500 (P1 100 x $45 + P2 700 x $30), forfeiting the $4,400 the vendor relationship adds.
ExplanationWrongB: Option B preserves the $29,900 total but swaps the story to outsourcing P1; the 100-unit contractual minimum forbids external sourcing of P1, and its $30-per-constraint-hour rank makes it the wrong product to move anyway.
ExplanationWrongD: Option D ships all 900 P2 units to the vendor and prints $31,100; the plan misallocates the constraint because in-house P2 earns the highest return per hour ($60), so displacing it sacrifices margin and strands the freed capacity behind lower-return P1 volume.
Stem: Two products share a 500-hour constraint. P1: CM $45, 1.5 hours per unit, contractual minimum 100 units. P2: CM $30, 0.5 hours per unit, demand 900 units. Vendor supplies P2 at an $8 premium. Optimal plan and total contribution?
Topic: C.200 Integrative capstone - constraint, floor, and vendor
VerifiedChecks: Independent: P1 floor 150h; P2 350h->700; outsource 200 P2 at 22 -> 29,900
